nameStory: The Arrowhead Orbweaver gets its name from its distinctive triangular abdomen that looks exactly like the pointed tip of an arrow or arrowhead. This unique shape makes it instantly recognizable among the typically round-bodied orbweaver family. The scientific name Verrucosa means 'warty' in Latin, referring to the small bumps dotting its triangular body.
description: The Arrowhead Orbweaver is a medium-sized spider with a dramatically pointed, triangular abdomen that sets it apart from all other orbweavers. Females display bright white or yellow coloring on their arrow-shaped abdomens, while the rest of the body is typically brown or gray. This distinctive spider builds the classic circular orb web but breaks orbweaver tradition by sitting upright in its web facing upward, rather than hanging head-down like most of its relatives. It's found across North America but is quite uncommon in New England.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The abdomen is dramatically triangular and pointed like an arrowhead - unmistakable among spiders. Run your eyes along the outline and you'll see sharp angles instead of the typical round, bulbous shape of other orbweavers.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Small wartlike bumps dot the triangular abdomen, giving it a textured appearance that would feel rough to the touch. Females show bright white or yellow coloring on the pointed abdomen.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds a classic circular orb web with sticky spiral threads, but the web feels notably stronger and more substantial than typical orbweaver webs when accidentally walked into.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Sits facing upward in the center of its web - a highly unusual position for orbweavers. Most orbweavers hang head-down, making this upright posture a key identifying behavior.

habitat: This spider can be found in gardens, woodland edges, and areas with mixed vegetation where it can anchor its webs between shrubs, tall grasses, or low tree branches. It prefers locations with some shelter from direct wind but enough open space to build its substantial circular webs. Look in areas where flying insects are abundant, as these provide the primary food source.

seasonality.spring: Young spiders may be seen establishing their first webs. Webs are smaller and the distinctive triangular shape may be less pronounced in juveniles.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when mature females are most visible in their webs. The bright white or yellow coloring on the triangular abdomen is most vivid during warm summer months.
seasonality.fall: Mating season when males may be found near female webs. Egg sacs are produced and females may become less active as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically don't survive freezing temperatures. The next generation overwinters as eggs in protected locations, waiting for spring warmth to emerge.

funFact: This spider uses a special hunting technique called 'reeling behavior' - when prey gets caught in its extra-strong web, it actually reels the victim in like a fisherman pulling in a catch, rather than just walking over to bite it like most spiders do.
confusionNotes: The dramatically pointed, triangular abdomen makes this spider nearly impossible to confuse with any other New England species. If you see a spider with a truly arrow-shaped body, you've found an Arrowhead Orbweaver - no other spider in our region has this distinctive silhouette.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being found across North America, this species is quite rare in New England with very few recorded sightings. Don't be disappointed if you never encounter one - many experienced naturalists have never seen this distinctive spider in our region.
compareHints: This is the only Verrucosa species in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other orbweavers like the Common Garden Spider or Marbled Orbweaver, the Arrowhead Orbweaver's triangular abdomen and upward-facing web position make it unmistakable. While other orbweavers have round, bulbous abdomens and hang head-down in their webs, this species breaks both rules with its sharp angles and upright posture.
